title: Single-cell omics & GWAS integration · Saturday, November 28

transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Single-cell omics & GWAS integration, for Saturday, November 28.
Let's turn to single-cell omics and GWAS integration, where today's papers move from asking which cell type to asking which cell state.

The headline paper is from the Stitziel lab in Nature, on the non-coding risk for coronary artery disease. The authors profiled coronary arteries from 44 donors with single-nucleus multiome and mapped 11,269 chromatin accessibility QTLs.
Variant effects changed across smooth muscle cell states, and with Hi-C, CRISPR interference and Perturb-seq, the paper goes past annotation to perturbation.

It names AMOTL2 as a smooth muscle-specific disease gene, and points to extracellular matrix remodelling as a core program. Forty-four donors is modest, though, so those state-dependent effects need replication.

The Parker lab paper in Nature Communications is much larger: 281 skeletal muscle biopsies. The authors split single-nucleus ATAC fragments into nucleosome-free regions and phased nucleosomes to sharpen the mapping.

They map about 76 thousand nucleosome-free region QTLs and 25 thousand nucleosome QTLs, with 1,528 cases where accessibility likely drives nucleosome positioning. Hundreds colocalize with GWAS signals for grip strength, atrial fibrillation and fasting insulin.

So both papers refine what a chromatin QTL means, by cell state or by fragment structure. Turning to immune cells, the Liu lab in Genes combined OneK1K single-cell eQTLs from 20 immune subsets with an asthma GWAS of about 122 thousand cases.
Using SMR and colocalization, they report 46 genes tied to specific cell subsets. At 17q21, ORMDL3 colocalizes in B cells, while GSDMB colocalizes in NK cells and CD8 effector memory T cells.
Half of those genes have tractability evidence, but nothing was perturbed, so the cell-type assignments are statistical inferences, not tested mechanisms.
Briefly, the Ma lab in Brain Sciences built a 325 thousand nucleus substantia nigra atlas and ranked microglia as the cell type most linked to Parkinson's risk.
The takeaway is that GWAS integration is moving from naming a cell type to pinning risk on specific cell states and programs, and experimental perturbation is what makes those claims convincing.
